summary: Updates the HTTP/2 specification to forbid TLS 1.3 post-handshake authentication, in the same spirit as the existing ban on TLS 1.2 renegotiation in HTTP/2. The goal is to avoid ambiguity about which requests a late authentication applies to. It was replaced by RFC 9113.

plainLanguage.summary: HTTP/2 does not allow a TLS 1.3 server to request a client certificate after the handshake, because the request could not be matched to one HTTP request. RFC 8740 updates RFC 7540 and was later replaced by RFC 9113.

subtitle: HTTP/2 forbids TLS 1.3 post-handshake certificate requests

tldr.problem: HTTP/2 multiplexes requests over one connection, so a client cannot match a certificate request after the handshake to the HTTP request that triggered it.
tldr.mechanism: HTTP/2 servers MUST NOT send TLS 1.3 post-handshake CertificateRequest messages, and clients treat them as PROTOCOL_ERROR connection errors.
tldr.outcome: RFC 8740 updates RFC 7540 and was later replaced by RFC 9113.

today: RFC 8740 updates RFC 7540 and has been obsoleted by RFC 9113.

sections.title: Why Post-Handshake Authentication Conflicts
sections.content:
TLS 1.2 and earlier support renegotiation, which can change connection parameters and keys or request a client certificate during a connection. HTTP/2 sends multiple HTTP requests over one connection, so a client cannot tell which request caused a certificate request. RFC 7540 therefore forbids renegotiation.

TLS 1.3 removes renegotiation but has a separate post-handshake authentication mechanism. The RFC says that mechanism creates the same problem for HTTP/2 and updates the HTTP/2 rule to forbid it.
sections.plainLanguage: HTTP/2 carries several requests at once on one connection. If a certificate request arrives later, the client cannot tell which request caused it, so the protocol forbids that request.

sections.title: The HTTP/2 Rule
sections.content:
HTTP/2 servers MUST NOT send post-handshake TLS 1.3 CertificateRequest messages. HTTP/2 clients MUST treat such a message as a connection error of type PROTOCOL_ERROR.

The rule applies even before the HTTP/2 connection preface. It also applies if the client offered the TLS post_handshake_auth extension, because that extension is advertised independently of the selected ALPN protocol and does not indicate support for HTTP/2 post-handshake authentication.
sections.plainLanguage: A server must not ask for a client certificate after the TLS handshake when using HTTP/2. If a client receives that request, it treats it as a PROTOCOL_ERROR connection error.

sections.title: Other TLS Messages and Status
sections.content:
TLS 1.3 KeyUpdate and NewSessionTicket messages are permitted after the handshake. HTTP/2 implementations MUST support key updates when TLS 1.3 is negotiated. NewSessionTicket is also allowed; the RFC says its interactions with HTTP when early data is enabled are defined by RFC 8470.

RFC 8740 updates RFC 7540. The unit metadata records RFC 9113 as the document that later obsoleted it.
sections.plainLanguage: The rule bans post-handshake certificate requests, not every post-handshake TLS message. KeyUpdate and NewSessionTicket remain allowed, and RFC 9113 later replaced RFC 8740.
